name: Red light therapy for eyes

lead: Red light therapy uses low-power red or near-infrared lights placed near the skin. Some looksmaxxing lists suggest using it around the eyes for a brighter, fresher eye area.

The suggested mechanism is light absorbed by an enzyme in mitochondria, which is thought to boost cell energy and circulation, though Wikipedia describes the effect as under investigation. The eye research cited in reference material concerns repeated low-level red-light treatment for juvenile myopia, a different goal. No study of cosmetic brightening of the eye area was found.

paras: People use LED masks, wands or panels held near the face for short sessions several times a week, over weeks. Some devices come with eye shields.
Mild irritation is reported, long-term effects are unknown, and eye protection is suggested for some devices. Ocular safety for cosmetic use is not established in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Users shine red light around the eyes in the hope that boosted cell energy and circulation leaves the eye area looking brighter and fresher. The eye research that exists concerns childhood myopia, not cosmetic effects.

lead: Red light therapy for the eyes, in looksmaxxing usage, means applying low-level red or near-infrared light to the eye area, meaning the thin skin around the eyes, with the aim of a fresher, brighter, smoother-looking periocular region. It belongs to photobiomodulation (formerly called low-level laser therapy), in which low-power lasers or LEDs deliver light to the body surface.[1] The eye area is where fine lines, crepey texture and a tired look tend to show first, so people who use light panels, masks or wands on the face often include it.

The generally accepted explanation is that the light is absorbed by an enzyme in the mitochondria, cytochrome c oxidase, which is thought to change cellular energy activity; Wikipedia describes the mechanism and effectiveness as still under investigation.[1] A 2023 split-face randomized controlled trial in 137 women aged 40 to 65 measured periocular wrinkle volume after 10 sessions of red or amber LED light over four weeks and reported reductions of roughly 30 percent on both sides, and a 2023 open study of a red LED mask in 20 women reported improvements in crow's feet depth and other skin measures.[2][3]

A separate line of ocular research concerns light delivered to the eye itself: repeated low-level red-light treatment has been studied for myopia in children, multiwavelength photobiomodulation has been tested in dry age-related macular degeneration, and a small study has looked at a consumer LED mask for dry eye.[1][4][5][5] Those involve clinical devices used under supervision or specific protocols and differ from skin-focused cosmetic panels and masks, and ophthalmologists have begun to publish on eye safety questions for home masks.[5][5]

paras: Photobiomodulation uses low-power lasers or LEDs at specific red and near-infrared wavelengths applied to the surface of the body, and several devices have US FDA clearance for particular uses.[1] Skin-focused panels, masks and wands are the usual form for the eye area. LED light penetrates shallowly, which suits skin-level targets such as the periocular region; Wikipedia notes that light penetration depends on wavelength and that visible red light of 650 nm reaches only a small fraction of its intensity at about 1.6 mm into the skin.[1]

The terminology is crowded. Wikipedia says Mester's original term was laser biostimulation, later low-level laser therapy and, after LEDs came into use, low-level light therapy, with photobiomodulation emerging as a synonym that industry professionals now prefer. Marketing also uses phrases such as red light therapy and cold laser therapy.[1]

Reviewers note that more than 50 years after the technique was discovered there is still no agreement on the parameters and protocols for clinical application, and the wide range of wavelengths, energies, powers, pulse modes and treatment durations has in some cases produced contradictory results.[6] That review also reported that tissues rich in mitochondria, such as muscle, brain, heart and nerve, tended to respond to lower doses of light than tissues with fewer mitochondria, such as skin, and that ineffective results in the studies it compared were more often associated with excessive dosing than insufficient dosing.[6]

Wikipedia states that photobiomodulation follows the Grotthuss-Draper principle, that light must be absorbed by a chemical before a photochemical effect can occur, and that the generally accepted target is cytochrome c oxidase, an enzyme in the mitochondrial electron transport chain.[1] A 2026 narrative review of ocular photobiomodulation describes mitochondrial mechanisms involving cytochrome c oxidase signalling, nitric oxide release, reactive-oxygen-species-driven hormetic responses and anti-inflammatory effects.[5]

Wikipedia also says that doses below a certain range do not appear effective and that excessive radiation could in principle produce singlet oxygen that damages cells.[1] The idea behind the cosmetic use is that stimulated skin cells, including fibroblasts, support collagen and repair processes, so that fine lines and texture around the eyes look better over weeks of repeated sessions.

Wikipedia credits the Faroese physician Niels Finsen, who used red light on smallpox lesions, as the father of modern light therapy; he received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[1] The biological effects of low-power lasers are credited to the Hungarian physician Endre Mester (1903-1984), who after the ruby laser (1960) and helium-neon laser (1961) appeared found that a faulty ruby laser that failed to shrink tumours in mice nonetheless made shaved mice regrow hair faster, published in 1967.[1] He later showed that low-level helium-neon light accelerated wound healing, treated skin ulcers in people in the 1970s, and founded the Laser Research Center at Semmelweis Medical University in Budapest in 1974.[1]

By 1987, Wikipedia says, laser companies were claiming benefits for pain, sports injuries and arthritis on limited supporting evidence.[1] The field then moved from lasers to LEDs as cheaper devices became available, and consumer panels, masks and combs are now sold for skin, hair and recovery use.[1] In 2025 a consensus statement in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology presented clinical recommendations for medical and aesthetic use, drawn up by a 21-member international panel.[7]

The eye area is one of the first places to show fine lines and tiredness, so red light is sometimes listed among tools for brightening it. People most often describe using a face panel or LED mask for a set number of minutes at a time, repeated over weeks, and combine it with a skincare routine such as retinoids, sunscreen and moisturiser. Home LED masks are marketed for the whole face, and the periocular skin is included in their coverage.

Some lifters on forums mention trying red light panels during recovery sessions, and one T Nation poster described covering his eyes for 10 minutes during a first session and planning to get protective glasses.[8] Eye shielding with goggles or the hands is a recurring practical point in such accounts.

Practitioners usually distinguish between skin-level use around the eyes, with the eyes closed or shielded, and the clinical ocular protocols used in eye clinics, which are delivered with specific devices under professional supervision.[4][5]

sections.h: Research on the eye area and skin
paras: The closest study to the cosmetic goal is a split-face randomized clinical trial from Brazil, published in Photobiomodulation, Photomedicine, and Laser Surgery in 2023, which enrolled 137 women aged 40 to 65 with skin phototypes II to IV. Each received 10 sessions over four weeks, with red light (660 nm) on one side of the face and amber light (590 nm) on the other, at the same dose of 3.8 J/cm2. Periocular wrinkle volume fell by about 31.6 percent on the red side and 29.9 percent on the amber side; hydration and viscoelasticity did not improve, and quality-of-life questionnaires improved.[2]

A 2023 paper in Skin Research and Technology described 20 women who used a red LED mask (630 nm, 12-minute sessions, twice a week for three months). The authors reported progressive improvement at one, two and three months in crow's feet depth, facial oval relaxation, firmness, dermal density and complexion, with benefits lasting up to a month after stopping; the authors were affiliated with the cosmetics company and device maker involved, and the abstract gives no numerical values.[3]
Wikipedia notes that for some uses, such as hair loss, reviews suggest red and infrared suit androgenetic alopecia, which shows that the choice of wavelength depends on the target tissue.[1]

Eye-directed photobiomodulation is a distinct field. In a 2024 randomized clinical trial in Ophthalmology, 192 children and adolescents with high myopia were assigned to repeated low-level red-light therapy or control; at 12 months axial length changed by about -0.06 mm in the treated group against 0.34 mm in controls, and spherical equivalent changed by 0.11 D against -0.75 D.[5]

The LIGHTSITE III trial tested multiwavelength photobiomodulation (590, 660 and 850 nm) in dry age-related macular degeneration. In the 13-month analysis of 100 participants (148 eyes), the treated group gained 2.4 more letters of best-corrected visual acuity than the sham group, and fewer treated eyes developed new geographic atrophy; the abstract describes a favourable safety profile.[4] A 24-month analysis has also been published.[9]

A retrospective study of 20 postmenopausal women with dry eye disease used a consumer LED beauty mask for 20-minute sessions on alternate days for three weeks and reported improved tear osmolarity, tear break-up time and symptom scores with no adverse events; the authors called the findings preliminary, citing small size and no control group.[5] A 2026 narrative review concluded that the biological rationale is plausible but that evidence is heterogeneous across devices, wavelengths and protocols, and it called for standardised randomized trials.[5]

According to Wikipedia, evidence is tentative for some musculoskeletal pain, supports use for preventing oral mucositis in certain stem-cell transplant patients, and is mixed for hair loss, with a 2017 review reporting improvement in 10 of 11 androgenic alopecia trials.[1] A 2025 consensus statement in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology, drafted by a panel of 21 experts through a systematic review and two Delphi rounds, states that red light photobiomodulation does not induce DNA damage and is a safe modality for adult patients, and lists effectiveness for peripheral neuropathy, androgenic alopecia, several kinds of wound ulcer and acute radiation dermatitis.[7]

Wikipedia suggests eye protection for some photobiomodulation devices.[1] In 2026 the American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports published a case of a 43-year-old woman who developed acute bilateral angle closure from ciliochoroidal effusions after about two weeks of home red-light-mask use; her vision returned to 20/20 in both eyes after the mask was stopped and she was treated, and the authors noted that such effusions had not previously been linked to home red-light use and called for further study of ocular safety.[5] The report is a single case.

Ocular treatment devices such as those in the macular degeneration trials are used under clinical supervision, and the myopia trials use specific clinical devices, which is a separate matter from skin devices.[4][5] The 2026 narrative review says short-term tolerability appears favourable while long-term safety is not well defined.[5]

A randomized controlled trial reported in Photobiomodulation, Photomedicine, and Laser Surgery in 2023 examined periocular wrinkle volume after photobiomodulation in 137 women, and as its title states reported a 30 percent reduction.[2] A 2023 paper in Skin Research and Technology reports on red LED mask use for signs of skin ageing in 20 women.[3]

For the eye itself, the LIGHTSITE III randomized, sham-controlled trial evaluated multiwavelength photobiomodulation in dry age-related macular degeneration at 13 and 24 months, a 2024 randomized trial studied repeated low-level red-light therapy in children with high myopia, and a small retrospective study looked at a consumer LED mask for dry eye.[4][9][5][5]

Wikipedia reports occasional mild pain or skin irritation, unknown long-term effects on skin, and suggests eye protection for some devices; it also notes that skin responses may vary by skin type and recommends dermatologist consultation, with only FDA-cleared devices suggested for dermatologic use in the US.[1] A 2023 systematic review cited there found no evidence that people with cancer or cancer risk should avoid photobiomodulation.[1]

Wikipedia records a regulatory case from this field: in 2014 the FDA sought an injunction against QLaser PMA over claims that its devices could treat more than 200 diseases including cancer, diabetes and HIV/AIDS, and a permanent injunction followed in 2015. The owner pleaded guilty in January 2018 to conspiracy to introduce misbranded medical devices and criminal contempt and was sentenced to 12 years.[1] Wikipedia also reports that Medicare does not cover low-level laser therapy and that some insurers cover it only for oral mucositis prevention.[1]

Related practices include LED face masks and panels for general skin ageing, red-light combs and caps for hair, eye-area devices such as microcurrent wands and cooling tools, and clinical light-based facial treatments.

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing and gym circles, red light for the eyes comes up as part of the wider LED mask and red-light panel trend for skin and recovery, with the eye area a frequent target for fine lines.[8]
